quizzes.title: Where the Sea Lies
quizzes.passage: The South China Sea lies in the Pacific region, alongside the mainland of South-East Asia. Several countries border its waters, and the sea is linked to neighbouring seas through passages at its edges. The sea lies within a maritime zone that is heavily trafficked, and a large portion of global trade moves through this zone every year. Its waters hold oil and gas deposits beneath the seabed, and they also support rich fishing grounds. Because of these resources and routes, the sea has become a focus of attention for the states around it. Its waters have also been the subject of long-running disputes, and many of these disputes concern islands scattered across the sea. Several of the islands are claimed by more than one state. International law provides a legal framework that seeks to balance the interests of coastal states and seafaring nations, though its interpretation in this sea remains fiercely disputed. Ships that move through these waters follow routes shaped by the passages at the sea's edges. In short, the sea is important for commerce, resources and regional security. The islands and waters at its centre have drawn repeated attention from governments in the region. This makes the sea a subject of continuing diplomatic effort.

questions.q: Which of the following countries is listed among those bordering the South China Sea?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists Brunei among the countries bordering the sea.

questions.q: Through which strait is the South China Sea linked with the Philippine Sea?
questions.explanation: The booklet says the Luzon Strait connects the South China Sea with the Philippine Sea.

questions.q: Which sea does the Taiwan Strait connect the South China Sea with?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the Taiwan Strait connects the South China Sea with the East China Sea.

questions.q:
Read the following assertion and reason.
Assertion (A): The South China Sea and the East China Sea together are termed the China Sea.
Reason (R): The Luzon Strait links the South China Sea with the East China Sea.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: A is correct, but the booklet links the Luzon Strait to the Philippine Sea, not the East China Sea.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Taiwan Strait   ->   A. East China Sea
II. Luzon Strait   ->   B. Philippine Sea
III. South China Sea and East China Sea   ->   C. China Sea
IV. South China Sea   ->   D. Arm of the Western Pacific Ocean
questions.explanation: The Taiwan Strait leads to the East China Sea, the Luzon Strait to the Philippine Sea, the two seas together form the China Sea, and the South China Sea is an arm of the Western Pacific Ocean.

questions.q:
Read the following statements about the sea's geography:
I. The Taiwan Strait links the sea with the East China Sea.
II. Thailand is among the countries bordering the sea.
III. Brunei is among the countries bordering the sea.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and III match the booklet, while Thailand is not in the booklet's list of bordering countries.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about the sea's geography are correct?
I. The sea is an arm of the Western Pacific Ocean.
II. Japan is among the countries bordering the sea.
III. The Luzon Strait connects the sea with the East China Sea.
questions.explanation: Only the first statement is correct, since the booklet describes the sea as an arm of the Western Pacific Ocean.

quizzes.title: Seas, Straits and Neighbours
quizzes.passage: The South China Sea is located in the Pacific region and lies alongside the mainland of South-East Asia. A number of countries surround its waters, and the sea connects with neighbouring seas through passages at its edges. Ships that travel through these passages move between the sea and the wider waters beyond it. The sea lies in a maritime zone that is heavily trafficked, and a large portion of global trade passes through that zone. Beneath its seabed are oil and gas deposits, and its waters support rich fishing grounds. Several islands within the sea are claimed by more than one country, and these overlapping claims have made the waters a site of long-running disputes. The sea's position matters for trade, energy and fishing, as well as for the governments whose coastlines face it. The interpretation of the international law of the sea remains fiercely disputed in this region. Routes through the passages carry a steady flow of commercial traffic. Its islands include several groups, and the booklet names them while describing the disputes. Its waters are shared by a number of governments, each of which has its own position on how the sea should be used. The sea therefore sits at the centre of questions about trade, energy and fishing.

questions.q: Which strait links the South China Sea with the Philippine Sea? (name the strait)
questions.explanation: The booklet says the Luzon Strait connects the South China Sea with the Philippine Sea.

questions.q: Which sea does the Taiwan Strait link the South China Sea with? (name the sea)
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the Taiwan Strait connects the sea with the East China Sea.

questions.q: Which ocean is the South China Sea described as an arm of? (name the ocean)
questions.explanation: The booklet describes the South China Sea as an arm of the Western Pacific Ocean.

questions.q: How many countries does the booklet list as bordering the sea? (give the number in figures)
questions.explanation: The booklet names seven bordering countries: Brunei, China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam.

questions.q: Which bordering country is listed first in the booklet's list of bordering countries? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet's list begins with Brunei, followed by China and Indonesia.

questions.q: Which bordering country is listed last in the booklet's list of bordering countries? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet's list ends with Taiwan and then Vietnam.

questions.q: Which bordering country is listed third in the booklet's list of bordering countries? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists Indonesia after Brunei and China.

quizzes.title: Resources and Trade of the Sea
quizzes.passage: The South China Sea contains deposits of oil and natural gas beneath its seabed, and those deposits have been estimated by a United States government agency. Its waters are also known for rich fishing grounds, and fishing vessels from several countries work in the area. The sea is part of a heavily trafficked maritime zone, and a large share of global trade moves through this zone. Ships crossing the sea carry goods between many ports, and the traffic on these routes is substantial. Because the sea holds resources and routes of this kind, it is a place of economic interest for the states around it. Several islands in the sea are claimed by more than one state, and the booklet notes that these claims overlap. Its waters have also been the subject of long-running disputes, which involve questions of energy, fishing and the rights of coastal states. Estimates of its resources are published figures, and they are presented as estimates rather than as certain amounts. Taken together, these features explain why the sea is discussed so often in international news. The sea's resources and routes therefore matter to the countries around it, and the disputes over its waters continue to shape how it is used.

questions.q: According to the US Energy Information Agency, how much oil is estimated to lie in deposits under the sea?
questions.explanation: The booklet cites the US Energy Information Agency for an estimate of 11 billion barrels of oil under the sea.

questions.q: Which agency estimated that over 21% of global trade passes through the sea?
questions.explanation: The booklet attributes the 21% trade estimate to UNCTAD.

questions.q: What does the booklet say about the sea's fishing vessels?
options: More than half of the world's fishing vessels operate in this area
About one-fifth of the world's fishing vessels operate in this area
None of the world's fishing vessels operate in this area
Fishing vessels are banned from the area
questions.explanation: The booklet states that more than half of the world's fishing vessels operate in this area.

questions.q:
Read the following assertion and reason.
Assertion (A): Ships passing through the sea add to its importance for global commerce.
Reason (R): Nearly one-third of the world's shipping trade passes through this waterway each year.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: The yearly share of shipping trade passing through the waterway explains why its traffic matters for global commerce.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Estimated oil deposits under the sea   ->   A. 11 billion barrels
II. Estimated natural gas deposits   ->   B. 190 trillion cubic feet
III. Share of the world's fisheries   ->   C. 12%
IV. Share of global trade (UNCTAD)   ->   D. Over 21%
questions.explanation: The booklet gives 11 billion barrels of oil, 190 trillion cubic feet of gas, 12% of world fisheries and over 21% of global trade.

questions.q:
Read the following statements about the sea's resources and trade:
I. The estimated oil deposits under the sea are 11 billion barrels.
II. The estimated natural gas deposits under the sea are 190 billion cubic feet.
III. Nearly one-third of the world's shipping trade passes through the sea each year.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: The gas estimate in the booklet is 190 trillion cubic feet, so statement II is wrong while I and III match the text.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about the sea's fishing and trade are correct?
I. The sea's fishing grounds are estimated to hold 12% of the world's fisheries.
II. UNCTAD estimates that over 21% of global trade passes through the sea.
III. The sea lies within the Indian Ocean.
questions.explanation: Statements I and II match the booklet, while the booklet places the sea in the Western Pacific rather than the Indian Ocean.

quizzes.title: Estimates and Shares
quizzes.passage: Beneath the sea's floor lie deposits of oil and natural gas, and estimates of their size have been published by an agency of the United States government. The waters are also a major fishing area, with rich grounds that support fleets from several neighbouring countries. The sea is part of a maritime zone that is heavily trafficked, and a large share of global commerce moves across it. Goods carried by ship through these waters travel between many ports, which makes the routes economically important. An international body that studies trade has also published figures on the share of world trade that passes through the sea. The sea's resources and routes are therefore valuable to the states around it. The waters have been the subject of long-running disputes, and several islands within them are claimed by more than one state. The disputes concern both the islands and the waters around them, and the sea also carries a large share of the world's shipping trade. Taken together, the resources, fishing grounds and shipping routes explain why the sea draws so much attention in international news. The booklet places these figures alongside its account of the sea's islands and disputes. The figures are reported as estimates, so they describe approximate amounts rather than exact totals.

questions.q: How much oil, in billion barrels, is estimated to lie in deposits under the sea? (number)
questions.explanation: The booklet gives the oil estimate as 11 billion barrels, citing the US Energy Information Agency.

questions.q: How much natural gas, in trillion cubic feet, is estimated in deposits under the sea? (number)
questions.explanation: The booklet gives the gas estimate as 190 trillion cubic feet.

questions.q: What share of the world's fisheries does the sea contain, in percent? (number)
questions.explanation: The booklet estimates that the sea holds 12% of the world's fisheries.

questions.q: What share of global trade passes through the sea, in percent? (number)
questions.explanation: The booklet says over 21% of global trade passes through the sea, according to UNCTAD.

questions.q: What is the estimated value of global trade passing through the sea, in trillion dollars? (number)
questions.explanation: The booklet puts the value of trade passing through the sea at $3.37 trillion.

questions.q: Which United States agency estimated the oil and gas deposits? (acronym)
questions.explanation: The booklet attributes the oil and gas estimates to the United States Energy Information Agency.

questions.q: Which United Nations body estimated the share of global trade passing through the sea? (acronym)
accept: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development
questions.explanation: The booklet attributes the trade share estimate to UNCTAD.

quizzes.title: Islands and Claims
quizzes.passage: Several islands and shoals in the South China Sea are claimed by more than one country, and many of these claims overlap. The Paracel Islands are one such group, and they lie in an area where a battle once took place. One larger island group is claimed by a bigger number of states than most other features in the sea, which makes it central to the disputes. Scarborough Shoal is another feature whose ownership is contested by several governments. Control of these features is not settled, and the claimant states have taken different positions on how the disputes should be resolved. The booklet notes that China has preferred bilateral negotiations with the other parties involved, and it records that China asserts historical rights to the sea. The overlapping claims shape the way the sea is governed, and each state's position affects the others. The claims are not only about land but also about the waters that surround each feature. The booklet also describes what these disputes mean for states beyond the region. Regional stability and freedom of navigation are central themes in this debate. These claims have been pursued over a long period, which is why the disputes are described as long-running.

questions.q: China has exercised de facto control of the Paracel Islands since 1974, following a battle involving which country?
questions.explanation: The booklet says the 1974 control followed the Battle of Paracel Islands, which involved South Vietnam.

questions.q: Which island group is claimed by China, Taiwan, Vietnam, Brunei and the Philippines?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists five claimants for the Spratly Islands, including Brunei and the Philippines.

questions.q: A 2012 standoff gave China de facto control over which region?
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the 2012 standoff resulted in China gaining de facto control over the Scarborough region.

questions.q:
Read the following assertion and reason.
Assertion (A): India has a stake in the security of the South China Sea.
Reason (R): A significant share of India's maritime commerce passes through the South China Sea and the Malacca Strait.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: India's maritime commerce passing through these waters is the reason the booklet gives for regional stability mattering to India.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Paracel Islands   ->   A. Claimed by China, Taiwan and Vietnam
II. Spratly Islands   ->   B. Claimed by China, Taiwan, Vietnam, Brunei and the Philippines
III. Scarborough Shoal   ->   C. Claimed by the Philippines, China and Taiwan
IV. Sea Lines of Communication   ->   D. Security could be threatened by greater Chinese militarisation
questions.explanation: The booklet matches each island group with its claimants and notes that Chinese militarisation could threaten Sea Lines of Communication.

questions.q:
Read the following statements about the island claims:
I. The Paracel Islands are claimed by China, Taiwan and Vietnam.
II. Brunei is among the claimants of the Paracel Islands.
III. China has exercised de facto control of the Scarborough region since 1974.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Only statement I matches the booklet, since Brunei does not claim the Paracels and the 1974 control refers to the Paracels, not Scarborough.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about India's interests in the sea are correct?
I. Greater Chinese militarisation could threaten the security of Sea Lines of Communication.
II. Chinese naval infrastructure in the sea could facilitate greater Indian Ocean power projection.
III. The Spratly Islands are claimed by India.
questions.explanation: Statements I and II match the booklet, while India is not listed among the claimants of the Spratly Islands.

quizzes.title: Claims and India's Stake
quizzes.passage: The South China Sea contains many islands, reefs and shoals, and several of them are claimed by more than one state. The claims overlap in several places, which means that the sea has been the focus of disputes for many years. One island group in the sea has been under the effective control of a single state since a battle fought in the 1970s, though other states still assert claims to it. A shoal near the Philippines has also been contested by several governments, and its status changed after a standoff. The islands and the waters around them are therefore part of a complex set of claims. The booklet notes that the claimant states have taken different positions on how the disputes should be settled. It also records that China has preferred bilateral negotiations with the other parties involved. Freedom of navigation and regional stability are important themes in the debate, and the booklet explains how these themes affect the countries that depend on the sea for their commerce. The overlapping claims shape the way the sea is governed, and each state's position affects the position of the others. These disputes have continued for a long time. Their history explains why the sea remains a focus of attention.

questions.q: In which year did a standoff give China de facto control over the Scarborough region? (year)
questions.explanation: The booklet states that a standoff in 2012 resulted in China gaining de facto control over the Scarborough region.

questions.q: China has held the Paracel Islands de facto since 1974, following a battle involving which country? (name the country)
questions.explanation: The booklet links China's control of the Paracels from 1974 to the Battle of Paracel Islands involving South Vietnam.

questions.q: Which group of islands is claimed by five states, including Brunei? (name the group, two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists China, Taiwan, Vietnam, Brunei and the Philippines as claimants of the Spratly Islands.

questions.q: Which shoal is claimed by the Philippines, China and Taiwan? (name the shoal, two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists the Philippines, China and Taiwan as claimants of Scarborough Shoal.

questions.q: Which island group is claimed by China, Taiwan and Vietnam? (name the group, two words)
questions.explanation: The booklet lists China, Taiwan and Vietnam as the claimants of the Paracel Islands.

questions.q: Apart from the South China Sea, through which strait does a significant share of India's maritime commerce pass? (name the strait)
questions.explanation: The booklet says a significant share of India's maritime commerce passes through the South China Sea and the Malacca Strait.

questions.q: What is the abbreviation for the sea routes that Greater Chinese militarisation could threaten? (abbreviation)
questions.explanation: The booklet warns that greater Chinese militarisation could threaten the security of Sea Lines of Communication.
